Where Are The Good Samaritans?

By [NAME]

We walk and drive past homeless people every day. Mostly, we do nothing.

Occasionally, stopped at a red light, we see a man approaching our car with a tattered cardboard sign asking for money to buy food. His proximity makes us nervous. His circumstances make us feel guilty.

We search for the smallest dollar bill we have. Avoiding too much eye contact, we lower the window just enough to slip the bill through.

As he begins to thank us, the light changes.

“Sorry, gotta go.”

And away we speed.

But where did we have to go? Home to dinner? To complain about the city? To ask why somebody has not done something about getting “those people” off the streets?

Somebody should. But perhaps that somebody includes us.

The Good Samaritan stopped, took responsibility, arranged care, and helped pay for it.

Where are today’s Good Samaritans?

Many already serve in shelters, congregations, recovery programs, and neighborhood organizations. Let us organize that compassion into a partnership with clear responsibilities and measurable results.

I propose “Good Sam”: a five-year partnership between government, religious institutions, and community organizations to address homelessness in Los Angeles and Ventura counties.

Government has a shared moral responsibility to help people get off the streets and restore safe public spaces.  I would support federal funding for this effort, with strict accountability, but....

Here is how Good Sam would work.

First, government would provide matching funds, coordination, and oversight. Participating agencies would help identify housing, coordinate services, establish financial controls, and maintain a public record of spending and results.

Second, participating religious institutions would match government financing dollar for dollar by “passing the basket” during services through designated, voluntary Good Sam collections. Every government dollar awarded to a participating institution would require a dollar raised for the program. Participation would be voluntary for institutions and individual donors. Congregations could pool their collections through a shared Good Sam fund, allowing smaller institutions to participate together. Government payments would follow verification of the required private match. This would give congregations a concrete responsibility: help finance the work, help carry it out, and help account for its results.

Third, religious and community partners would organize practical support: meals, transportation, apartment furnishings, identification documents, employment assistance, and regular personal contact. Each organization would accept specific assignments within its capabilities.

Fourth, qualified professionals would provide case management, mental health care, and addiction treatment. Each person enrolled would have an assigned case manager and an individual plan for housing, care, and greater stability. Volunteers would receive training and support. They would strengthen professional services, with clear boundaries and someone responsible for following through.

Fifth, the public would see the results. Reports would track dollars spent, verified matching contributions, housing placements, housing retention, and connections to needed care. Independent audits would examine spending. Ineffective providers would face corrective action or replacement, while participants’ care continued.

The partnership would serve people regardless of faith. Nobody would have to pray, attend worship, or accept religious instruction to receive assistance. Public dollars and matching contributions would support authorized homeless services, with separate accounting from religious activities.

To those whose first response is to complain about “Church and State” before considering the people we could help, I would answer, " This is a proposed, simple, local, and temporary partnership to help mitigate or solve one human dilemma.  It's not attempting to set new government precedent.   

Serious questions deserve serious answers. Good Sam would have written safeguards, voluntary participation, equal access, and transparent finances. We can respect religious freedom while welcoming religious institutions willing to help their neighbors.

The five-year commitment would allow time to build partnerships and measure whether people remain housed. Annual reviews would guide improvements. At five years, the program would expire unless renewed after an independent evaluation and public review.

The goal would be fewer people returning to homelessness year after year.

Safe sidewalks, accessible businesses, and usable parks matter. So does the human being sleeping outside them. Moving someone to another block accomplishes little without a path toward stability.

No honest person can guarantee that one program will end every instance of homelessness. We can demand a plan that connects money, personal responsibility, qualified care, and lasting housing.

We can also stop treating compassion as something we outsource entirely to government.

Pass the basket. Recruit the volunteers. Assign the case managers. Open the books. Measure the results.

The next light will turn green. We will have somewhere to go.

Let us help our homeless neighbors find somewhere to go, too.

Where are the Good Samaritans?

Let the answer begin with us.

The next time our PECO or PPL bill shows up higher than expected, remember this: a big chunk of the extra cost comes from cryptocurrency mining and the broader energy surge it drives.

In a conversation I had with former U.S. Bankruptcy Judge David R. [NAME] — who oversaw several major cryptocurrency bankruptcy cases, including Core Scientific (one of the largest crypto miners) — we both agreed: crypto functions, in practice, not as a currency but as a commodity whose worth is fundamentally based on the cost of the electricity needed to produce it. Judge [NAME] saw this reality up close while managing the financial wreckage of collapsed mining and crypto lending operations.

₿ Bitcoin isn’t “digital gold.” It is a commodity whose value is directly tied to the massive amounts of electricity required to mine it. Miners only make money if they can sell their Bitcoin for more than it costs to produce — and electricity is by far the biggest cost. As more bitcoins are mined, the network becomes harder to solve, so each new Bitcoin requires more electricity than earlier ones. [NAME] investors understood this dynamic: they were betting that Bitcoin’s price would keep rising as the power needed to mine the next coin grows higher. The more expensive it becomes to produce, the higher the price must go for miners to stay profitable. That’s why Bitcoin now trades in roughly the same range as the current cost to mine it — around $80,000.

Cryptocurrency mining now consumes between 0.6% and 2.3% of all electricity in the United States — roughly the same amount used by entire states like Washington or West Virginia. Because electricity demand is relatively inelastic in the short term, this added load has helped push our power bills up by 5–10% in many PJM areas through higher base rates and capacity charges. 

Here in PA-6, where families already stretch paychecks amid high housing costs and inflation, electricity prices are climbing. Recent rate increases, driven in part by surging demand from cryptocurrency mining operations across PJM, are hitting households hard. Utilities are upgrading infrastructure and securing more capacity, and guess who pays? Not just the miners or tech giants — we do, through higher base rates that don’t care whether we own crypto or not. In other words, when we look at our next PECO or PPL bill, 5–10% of it could be going to support cryptocurrency mining.

Beyond higher bills, the environmental toll is severe. Crypto mining’s explosive electricity demand is keeping older coal-fired plants running longer and increasing carbon emissions across the PJM region, where new load is often met by coal and natural gas. In PJM, this creates “carbon leakage”: demand from crypto operations pulls more coal-generated power from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia, raising local emissions and worsening air quality for Chester and Berks County families.

Right here in Pennsylvania, operations like the Scrubgrass and Panther Creek waste-coal plants have ramped up burning specifically to feed crypto mining, spiking sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and CO₂ output. Globally, Bitcoin mining alone has been equivalent to burning tens of billions of pounds of coal in emissions impact. This isn’t clean innovation — it’s dirty externalities that all Pennsylvanians breathe and pay for.

The late Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett’s longtime partner and one of the clearest thinkers in American business, cut through the hype years ago. He called Bitcoin “stupid,” “evil,” and something that makes its promoters look bad in comparison to honest work. Munger warned that it undermines sound money and creates massive externalities. He was right. We’re all subsidizing a speculative asset that delivers no goods, no services, and no productivity — just higher bills and dirtier air for the rest of us.

Blockchain technology has legitimate uses: secure supply chains, fraud-resistant records, efficient contracting in specific industries. Those applications deserve support. But proof-of-work crypto mining — the dominant model for Bitcoin — is different. It turns kilowatt-hours into lottery tickets, and Pennsylvania ratepayers and taxpayers are footing part of the tab while the grid strains and emissions rise.

Now comes the latest proposal in Washington: the BITCOIN Act, introduced by Senator Cynthia Lummis and Representative [NAME]. This legislation directs the Treasury to purchase 1 million Bitcoins over the next five years — 200,000 BTC per year — and hold them for at least 20 years. At current prices, that’s a government commitment of roughly $80 billion in new purchases on top of the hundreds of thousands of BTC already held from forfeitures.

The bill claims this spending is “budget-neutral,” but the mechanism is clear: it diverts the first $6 billion per year in Federal Reserve remittances — money that currently helps reduce the federal deficit or fund general government operations — straight into buying Bitcoin. In plain terms, Washington wants to redirect tens of billions of taxpayer-backed dollars to stockpile a volatile digital commodity whose rising price is fueled by the very electricity demand driving up our utility costs here in Pennsylvania.

Pennsylvanians are practical people. We want real innovation, reliable and affordable energy, and a government that doesn’t pick winners with our money. Crypto mining fails that test. It raises costs for families, manufacturers, and small businesses across Chester and Berks Counties while delivering concentrated gains to a narrow group of speculators — all while adding to our environmental burden.

We should welcome genuine technological progress — including efficient blockchain uses that don’t torch the grid or the atmosphere. But we must stop forcing every Pennsylvania household to subsidize Bitcoin’s appetite. Our grid, our air, and our tax dollars belong to all of us, not to the loudest promoters of digital gold. It’s time for policies that protect ratepayers, the environment, and fiscal responsibility first.

That’s why I’m running for Congress in PA-6. Families in West Chester, Downingtown, Reading, and across Chester and Berks Counties deserve a Representative who will fight to protect our wallets, our grid, and our air — not someone who rubber-stamps Washington schemes that drive up our electric bills and dirty our communities. We need practical leadership that puts Pennsylvania ratepayers and working families first: affordable and reliable energy, real fiscal responsibility, and innovation that doesn’t force us to subsidize speculative gains. I’m running to bring common sense back to Congress so our tax dollars and electric bills work for us — not for Bitcoin miners and their allies in Washington.
